Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the government to the contents of a letter I have just received from the citizens of Vancouver:
Dear Sir,-
We are desirous of going into the Peace River district in the early spring and find upon making enquiries that there is no settlers' rate from here, but at Blaine an American citizen can secure a settlers' rate. There is no reduction on settlers' effects from here but there is from the American side. .
We understand the Canadian government will bring a European in here for about $15, and to go from here costs us each $45 via C.N.R.
I know of at least one dozen good fellows who would go out there and would make good but all feel the big drawback it is to be a Canadian. The European and American has us backed off our own map.

The house resumed from Friday, February 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Usley for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to add my congratulations to those which have already been extended to the mover and seconder of the address and to compliment them upon the admirable manner in which they performed their duty.
I was very pleased to read the speech from the throne, for I can endorse the statements
made about the prosperity of Canada at the present time. I regret, however, that, speaking for my own province of Manitoba, last year conditions were not so satisfactory as they might have been. We were promised a very fine crop almost up to the time of harvest, but then rust attacked the crop and reduced materially both the yield and the grade. So that from the point of view of grain-raising it was not a great year for Manitoba. But I am pleased to be able to point out to the house that my province has to some extent ceased to be an exclusively grain-growing province. Mixed farming is largely carried on to-day, and through the sale of farm products, other than grain, our farmers there will not be in as difficult a position as they might have found themselves had they been relying entirely on graingrowing. I look upon this as a step in the right direction, for I think it will lead to the consolidation and prosperity of the whole farming community if more closely followed in the days that are to come.
During the short time I shall occupy the attention of the house I intend to take up the question with which I am more immediately concerned, namely, immigration. This has been a subject of considerable criticism during the last few months and in the press as well as in public speeches made by prominent individuals almost everywhere in the Dominion the matter has been discussed. There does not seem to be any unanimity in the ideas that have been expressed. You will find contradictory statements on the subject. It is said sometimes that the Department of Immigration is doing nothing, that no immigrants are coming in, and the suggestion is made that the door should be left wide open to allow all and sundry to enter Canada. Again, we find people complaining of the regulations as being too restrictive; the statement is made that the department is more restrictive than anything else in its operations. It is not very easy to form any opinion or to come to any conclusion regarding the criticisms which one reads and hears. One must simply come to one's best judgment by following closely the trend of events.
I came to this country a great many years ago as an immigrant, going west and taking part in public activities there in so far as they had to do with the opening up of a new country. We had a large inflow of immigration into western Canada and when I came to the department I fancied I knew a good deal about immigration and that perhaps I should be able to do some useful work in that direction. I have found, however, with larger experience and after coming more
The Address-Mr. Forke

closely into contact with the work as it is actually carried on, that there are a great many angles from which this question is to be viewed. I discovered that I had a good many things to learn before I should know everything regarding immigration into this new land of ours. I found no unanimous opinion anywhere. I am free to tell the house that scarcely a day passes that I do not receive letters blaming the department for not opening the door wide enough, while on the other hand I receive fetters of complaint regarding the unemployment of Canadians although foreigners come in to take the place of our own natives. This is about the situation as it exists to-day so far as criticism is concerned.
I listened with a great deal of attention and, I may add, much pleasure to the speech delivered by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). The hon. member for West Calgary suggested that nothing was being done, that immigration was dwindling, notwithstanding the fact that we had the facilities for taking care of a population of 17,000,000. He said that there were 10.000,000 acres of arable land within twenty miles of railway communication. In the main these statements may be true, but I am pretty sure that when the hon. member makes the statement that there are 10,000,000 acres of arable land within twenty miles of a railway he knows that these lands are all occupied by or are in the possession of private individuals or public corporations and that it requires money to purchase such land. So that settlers coming into the country without the means of purchasing stock and implements and making necessary payments on their land are in no position to take advantage of what is offered in the way of vacant lands. This is perhaps one of the great difficulties we have to face in connection with the whole question of immigration. It is not impossible to-day to secure any number of immigrants; people in every country on the face of the globe are looking with longing eyes towards this Dominion. If the doors were wide open and it were made possible for all and sundry to come in we should have no difficulty in securing immigrants. But of what advantage would it be to have innumerable immigrants landing on our shores without the means of setting up for themselves on the land? Our own labourers would also object strenuously to any such immigration policy. I have read the speeches of prominent citizens, bank presidents and others, in which advice is given on the question of immigration, and the leader of the opposition the other day suggested that the question should be taken hold

of and dealt with in a comprehensive way: vast sums of money ought to be spent. I have also heard that sort of statement made by bank presidents. I have never yet heard, however, any suggestion as to the manner in which the government should set about it and I have no authority from the government, nor do I think anyone else has at the present time, to spend vast sums in settling immigrants in this Dominion.
The activities of the department have been directed towards increasing the flow of people who are able to settle on the land and engage in agriculture. I was astonished the other day to read a statement attributed to Sir Charles Gordon in an address he delivered at the annual luncheon of the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association at Quebec. The report reads:
Spending thousands of dollars annually to assist immigration was a policy opposed by Sir Charles.
"Provide plenty of diversified employment here and you need not spend a single dollar to assist immigration", he said.
"It is impossible and nonsensical for us to think that an immigration policy for putting people on the land is going to be a successful policy for this country", he said. "It cannot be done.
If that is so, the activities of the department are in large part wasted, because it is one of our endeavours to secure people who will come into the Dominion and cultivate the soil and help to develop our natural resources. I may refer to the steadv flow of rural people towards the cities. This is not peculiar to Canada; it is a movement that is taking place throughout the world. And it is a problem with which it is quite difficult to cope. It is no satisfaction to me, and I am sure it is no satisfaction to anybody else, to see a foreign family coming in and taking the place of a good Canadian family who are obliged to move to the city; and this has taken place in numerous instances. Just how is this tendency to be stopped? It seems to me that it is a matter of remuneration. Love of country life is a sentiment that seems to be non-existent. Ownership of land does not appeal to the people of Canada as it does to the people of the old country; it does not appeal to our own native citizens as it does to the foreigner. I have heard of one foreigner who came to Canada and who, after taking up his 160 acres, went down on his knees in his farm and kissed the soil. Love of the soil is apparently entirely absent from the economic condition of our country to-day. And yet no country has ever been great, no country has endured whose roots were not firmly .planted in the

The Address-Mr. Forke
soil. This is one of the great problems we have before us in Canada to-day-how to make our rural people contented.
I do not think I should ever have been in the House of Commons had it not been for my desire to do something to help the rural population and to make this country something more worth seeking than it has been. Most people agree to-day that an increased population would be beneficial. Canada is a land of vast distances and of great undeveloped resources, only needing capital and population. We have railways enough. I agree with the leader of the opposition that we have sufficient railway accommodation to take care of a population of 17,000,000. And we have a great deal of vacant land. We have also schools, churches, roads, bridges and various other conveniences which I am sure could be utilized by a much larger population than we have to-day. At the same time we are up against the problem I have referred to. We sometimes hear of manless land and landless man. I would say, bring the man to the land and it will solve the problem. That is not the big problem. There are much more difficult problems to be solved. It has often been said that a satisfied immigrant is the best immigration agent. I am sure I have often called the attention of the house to the fact that in order to make immigration a success one of the first and most necessary things is to see that the people we have are satisfied and that the people who come will be satisfied. The leader of the opposition says that the department is doing nothing. I might at least indicate the lines we are following. The Trades and Labour Council delegation appeared before the Prime Minister and members of the government to present their finding at the annual convention. The memorandum was prefaced by a quotation from a speech of my own, and I felt honoured when I found the labour men coming to the government with a quotation from a speech which I had made. With the permission of the house I will read the quotation :
The reasons against a wide-open policy allowing the entry of all races and classes are convincing. Mere numbers of themselves would contribute nothing to Canada's prosperity. Idle men without means are never an economic asset, and may, on the contrary, become a very heavy drag upon the producing part of the population. It is essential that immigrants coming to this country, come not only to Canada but to employment. It is equally essential that in finding employment for themselves they do not displace others.
I made1 that speech in Toronto and it was reported in the Toronto Globe. I will quote a few lines from the statement of policy I made in another place. I said:
1.	To recognize that while Canada requires increased population, quality rather than quantity is of first importance-in other words, that our immigrants must be selected with a view to their mental, physical, moral, industrial and racial fitness for settlement in Canada.
2.	That limitation of numbers must be determined by the available supply of suitable classes and Canada's power of absorption.
3.	That British immigration must always hold
first place in importance and every legitimate effort used to increase the flow of people from the mother country.	'
4.	Next after British immigration encouragement should be offered to a movement of settlers from the United States and from northwestern Europe-of those healthy, hardy people desirous of establishing themselves on land in Canada and becoming absorbed in our national life.
That, broadly, is the policy of the Department of Immigration. There is no wide, allembracing and vast expenditure of money mentioned in any of those statements. I do not think the time has yet come for any such movement. I wish I had time to say a few words in regard to the visit I had the opportunity of making during the past summer to the Scandinavian countries, especially Norway, Sweden and Denmark. I had the privilege of meeting members of the government in all three of those countries, I received the most cordial reception and I found that they were very much interested in Canada;
I also found no difficulty in conversing with them, as all were able to speak good English, and could even understand English when spoken with a Scotch accent. They were all interested in Canada. Most of them understood that we were not anxious for a large immigration from the large cities of Europe. I remember the minister in Sweden saying " We have lots of people in our large cities, but I know you are not looking for them." He also said they had quite a large surplus of rural population, and added, " If they do not emigrate they will go to the cities, and we would rather see them emigrate than make trouble in our larger cities on account of unemployment ".
I found the same condition in Copenhagen. They had there the problem of people crowding to the cities, with resultant unemployment. They also had a large surplus in the rural population, young men growing up on the small farm, who had to move out and must find a home some other place-either go to the city or emigrate. After I saw those officials the Danish government gave me and my deputy a car in Copenhagen, and we

drove a great many miles through the country, visiting different farms. We talked with the people about their economic conditions, and I must say that I was delighted to meet the class of people I saw in those countries. They were frugal, industrious and intelligent, and we could find no better settlers to come to Canada and help develop this great country.
Reference is sometimes made to the immigration to Canada during the early years;
281.890	of the 1913 immigrants were from foreign countries, as against an immigration of 72,887 foreigners last year. A great many people have been very much exercised over the immigration which took place last year. To be fair, I think when the leader of the opposition was speaking he did not so much regret the number as the fact that the British immigration was outnumbering the foreign immigration.
The foreign outnumbering the British.

Yes, and a good many
people seem to be afraid we were getting too many foreigners, and yet in 1913 there were
281.890	foreigners.

What was the total
number?

The total number was
402,432 immigrants coming into Canada in 1913. This is sometimes mentioned to me as something we ought now to aim at. I do not agree with that opinion. The conditions in the earlier years of this century and the conditions that exist at the present time are not the same in any way. The period from 1901 to 1911 was an era of great railway building, something we shall never see the like of again on the North American continent. Thousands of miles were being built, British capital was flowing into the country, two and a half billions of British money, came into Canada during those years and tremendous areas of the richest agricultural land in the world was being opened up for settlement from the building of the railway in the western provinces. Immigrants were coming in and towns and villages were springing up everywhere. Work could be had by everyone who came to the country, and consequently the country was able at that time to absorb a very large number of immigrants. The conditions to-day are entirely different.
I am inclined to think that a good part of the immigration that came to Canada at that time was only loaned labour from Europe, because it is well known that during all those years money orders and cheques were continually going back to the countries from which

those people came. When the era of railway building was ended a great many people went back to Europe and their labour was simply available for the years they were here. But conditions are different now. Our country offers splendid opportunities for the right class of people. I do not want to discourage anyone who wishes to come to Canada with the proper ambition and fitness for the work he shall be engaged in when he comes here. However, I want to take exception to the statement of the leader of the opposition that immigration is dwindling. That statement is rather misleading. In comparison with 1913 I would say "yes," but when compared with recent years I would answer "no."
I have some statistics here which show how immigration is related to economics. When deflation came in the price of agricultural products after the war, farmers were very much discouraged. Immigration fell off in 1922, although for a time after the war, when high prices were still maintained we had one or two very good years. However, the slump came and the prices of agricultural products were entirely out of parity with the prices of what the farmers had to purchase. Those engaged in agriculture at that time could see nothing but ruin staring them in the face. Fortunately a change for the better came, and prospects are very much brighter and very much more encouraging at the present time. Although in 1921 there were 130,569 immigrants into Canada, the following year the number dropped to 89,999. In 1922 there came from Great Britain, the United States, and northern Europe 68,365 persons, and from other countries 21,634, a total of 89,999. In 1923 there came from Great Britain, the United States and northern Europe-I group these countries because the people from those lands are very easily assimilated; they are people very much like our own and constitute the very best immigrants-56,515 persons, and from other countries 16,372 immigrants, a total of 72,887. Now let me compare the figures for 1921, 1922, 1923 with those of 1926 and 1927. These periods are for eleven months.

So that in 1927 we had 81,428 more immigrants than in the twelve months of 1923. It is said that figures can be made to prove almost anything. The figures used by the leader of the opposition were perfectly correct, but they were presented in a different manner from the way I am giving them. I think the figures as I am giving them present a better view of the situation.
You manage yours better.

I have already stated that
the main endeavour of the government has been to secure British immigration. I have heard complaints sometimes that our display in London is not one for Canadians to be very proud of. I am quite willing to admit that we do not make as large a display in London as some of the other dominions do. I hope, however, that in the near feature we shall be able to do a little more than we have done in the past. But I must remind the house of this fact:	It is sometimes forgotten that the other dominions concentrate all their efforts in London itself, whereas we, on the other hand, have ten agencies throughout provincial England. At each of these ten points there is a resident agent with an office and staff where propaganda in behalf of immigration is in progress all the time. Lectures are given during the winter months, and members of the staff are available all the time for the purpose of advising intending immigrants. On my last visit to England I inspected all these agencies, and found them well equipped in every way. In each case the office is situated on the main street, and there is an attractive window display of Canadian products. Our efforts along this line are sometimes forgotten by visitors from Canada who simply go to London and see what is done there in connection with the other dominions. I think, perhaps, upon the whole that Canada carries on a more active propaganda for British immigration than any other dominion in the empire.

Do you seek to attract
the agricultural population of England, or the industrial population?

Anyone in Great Britain
'who passes the required moral and physical tests, and can pay his own passage money, is free to comq to Canada; there is no restriction debarring him from doing so. Any British subject is free to come to Canada; he does not even require a passport. On the other hand you need a passport when you want to enter Great Britain.

- I read in Saturday's paper that a British subject desiring to come to Canada had to answer ninety-four questions, but that no such questions were asked of continental immigrants. I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend. My desire is simply to get information on this subject, and the hon. gentleman may answer the questions as he proceeds with his address.

That could only refer to
assisted immigrants, and it is not correct even in the case of those who are given assisted passages. It is one of those instances in which there is a certain amount of truth, but it is presented in such a way as to be absolutely misleading.

That seems to be the
trouble.

I might take this opportunity of giving a brief explanation here of the empire settlement and other schemes. First of all let me read a short extract from the act, explanatory of the purpose of the legislation:
It shall be lawful for the Secretary of State, in association with the government of any of His Majesty's dominions, or with public authorities or private organizations either in the United Kingdom or in any part of such dominions, to formulate and co-operate in carrying out schemes for affording joint assistance to suitable persons in the United Kingdom who intend to settle in any part of His Majesty's oversea dominions.
An agreed scheme under this act may be either:-
(a)	a development or a land eettlement
scheme; or	.
(b)	a scheme for facilitating settlement in or migration to any part of His Majesty's oversea dominions by assistance with passages, initial allowances, training or otherwise:
And here is a clause which is rather serious:
The Secretary of State shall not agree to any scheme without the consent of the treasury.
That is the snag I ran up against when I was in Great Britain; I had to deal with the treasury. When you have to do with the immigration authorities you do not experience much trouble, but when you come to deal with the treasury the matter is a little more difficult.
I should like to say a few words in regard to assisted passages. Assisted passages are only for agriculturists and domestics, and the department has a system for nominating individuals or families who are to receive assisted passages. Nominations are made by the department, or by individuals in Canada who require agricultural or domestic help, or by department officials in Great Britain.
There is the matter of bulk nominations This refers to bringing over settlers in large
The Address-Mr. Forke

groups by any recognized transportation, colonization, religious or social organization approved by the department. This applies to bringing out to Canada single Britishers or British families who will come to this country to work on the land, and organizations responsible for their arrival in Canada must guarantee to find them farm work for one year after their arrival here. After those concerned have discovered where openings exist for the employment of agricultural help from the old land, they turn in a list of the prospective employers and the estimated number of workers required to the nearest office of the land settlement board for approval. When this approval is given the workers may then be secured and brought to Canada. This is where all the trouble in regard to immigration and the criticism one reads about arrives. When one reads something terrible about the Immigration department, this refers not to the general run of British immigrants but to the assisted immigrants who come over here on payment of ten dollars and whose families, under seventeen years of age, come over free.
I may point out that at this time the two governments, the Dominion government and the Imperial government, with a refund from the transportation companies, are paying the balance of the assisted passage rates. The people who are given these rates state that they are coming out to assured employment, to work on the land, or to buy farms and settle upon them. The Dominion of Canada through the Immigration department is paying out hard cash to bonus those people to come and work on the land, and I do not see why there should be any criticism or fault found because the department takes some steps to make sure that those applications are bona fide, and that the applicants are coming to assured employment on the land or at least to be employed in agricultural pursuits.
Who guaranteed the employment of the hundreds of Slovaks that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company flooded the west with last year?

I shall have a word to say later in regard to the railway agreement. I have often pointed out to officials of my department that you can get a man in Great Britain to promise that the transaction is perfectly straightforward. You know that a man is going out to work for a certain farmeT on this side; but when he comes he finds that he and his employer are entirely incompatible, they cannot get along, and of course when a man is anxious to leave he leaves. I do not 
know that there is any recourse in such a case; this is a weakness in the scheme and it is not very easily got over. It will, however, be noticed that newspapers and public speakers who criticize the department, criticize it not so much for that as for the restrictions and blocks that are put in the way of people doing just what I have spoken about. What satisfaction is it to the Dominion of Canada to get immigrants to come to Canada at ten dollars a head and then find that they come to Canada for no other purpose than to cross the line just as soon as possible? I want hon. members- to understand something about the difficulty encountered by the officials of my department, and. how hard it is to meet situations which arise and which they know cannot always be explained in public. The British people are like the Canadian people; they are a fine people; but at the same time there are in Great Britain a few who are quite willing to come to Canada at the expense of the Canadian government on a payment of ten dollars apiece, and who will slip over into Uncle Sam's territory just as soon as they can. It is the duty of the department to prevent that sort of thing as far as possible.
In connection with the Department of Immigration we have a land settlement board, the personnel of which is exactly the same as that of the soldier settlement board, although we have not as many employees as we had at one time. Their duties are to assist immigrants who come to this country and to look after the carrying out of the three-thousand family scheme. In fact they are supposed to be at the service of every immigrant who comes into this country, and to give advice and assistance in buying land, implements and stock, and in fact advice in general. I think it will be found that those men are doing splendid service throughout the Dominion in connection with land settlement work.
We have also a scheme for bringing boys over to this country. The Dominion government and the Imperial government give a grant of eighty dollars for every boy between fourteen and seventeen years of age coming from a good home, and we are working in co-operation with the provincial government in regard to this scheme. The provincial governments of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Manitoba have come under this scheme and they are at the present time working in agreement with the Dominion authorities. The province provides the farm as a sort of centre to which these boys come; it is not supposed to be a place where they will stay for any length of time; it is merely a dis-

Mr. MacLaren
tributing centre giving the Dominion government time to find suitable farms for these boys. The provincial government provides ten dollars, the Dominion government ten dollars and the Imperial government twenty dollars, making a fund of forty dollars for expenses in connection with the handling of these boys, and it must be remembered that the Imperial government and the Dominion government have made a grant of eighty dollars which is ample to cover the passage money of these boys as fifty-five dollars or sixty dollars will pay for the passage. This is one of the best schemes we have undertaken in the Immigration department, and we are getting hundreds of boys between fourteen and seventeen years of age, not from institutions but from good homes. These boys are under the protection of the provincial government, and I believe in a few years when they grow up into young manhood they will be the very pick of our Canadian citizens. This is one of the most hopeful endeavours in which we are engaged at the present time.

Do I understand
the minister aright, that all boys of this class come from private homes?

Most of the boys who are
being brought over under this scheme come from private homes. I would not say they are all coming from private homes. We have corporations like the corporation of the city of Newcastle which has been engaged in this work and sending some boys who are selected from private homes. They are young boys who do not know where to go to look for work and this scheme appeals to them. I had the pleasure of talking to the Lord Mayor of Newcastle who was most enthusiastic and who pointed out to me numbers of good families who had boys to whom this scheme appealed particularly. Most of the boys are of this character. I am not dealing with some of the private institutions which can avail themselves of the assisted passage scheme. The Salvation Army are bringing out a number of boys who get exactly the same grant as those who are coming out to the provinces. There are other organizations that have farms in Great Britain where they are doing a certain amount of training. Continual pressure is being brought to bear by different organizations, more especially by church organizations, to be allowed to come under this scheme, so that they may bring boys out to a centre from which they can be distributed. We have not encouraged them because we believe the provincial government with their farm have the best centre from which work of this kind can be carried
on. I have been particularly anxious to get into close cooperation with the different provincial governments in connection with all our immigration schemes and endeavours, and I believe the solution of many of our difficulties will be reached when we have the hearty cooperation, assistance and advice of our different provincial governments in connection with the activities of the federal Department of Immigration.

Mr. Speaker, before this debate
closes there are some matters, three in all, to which I desire to make reference. The first is one to which my attention was recently drawn, and I now bring it before hon. members of the house. I may term it the incorrect orientation of Canada as presented by the cartographers of the government, or the geographical malposition of our country as shown on the maps.
The correct projection of a map shows the lowest part of the latitudinal line opposite the centre of the lower border, and the terminals of each latitude should be an equal distance from the lower comers. But what do we find? I have here the Year Book of 1926, and I ask hon. members to inspect the map opposite the first page. They will find that the latitude of forty-five degrees on the east side is seven hundred miles from the bottom, while on the west side it is only one hundred and fifty miles; in other words, the eastern portion of Canada is shown five hundred and fifty miles farther north than its true position. This same error will be-found in the maps on pages 6, 17, 190 and 268. As a result of this the maritime provinces are projected to the north. The map is askew; the east is slewed up towards the north, and the province of Ontario and the western provinces are correspondingly depressed. One marvels that the city of Ottawa should have such cold winter weather when the cartographers have succeeded in placing Ontario so far south. The peculiar construction of the map, however, may throw some light on the chart which the Prime Minister used to speak about a few years ago.
The next example is found in a book issued by the Department of the Interior, and one produced at great expense-the Atlas of Canada, of 1915. Here there are at least six maps improperly constructed in the manner I have described. I presume that this atlas is now no longer being issued and therefore I refrain from making an analysis. I now refer to the map of 1924 issued by the Department of the Interior. It shows the same errors as those that I have mentioned. It

places my own city of St. John thirty miles north of Winnipeg, yet its true latitude runs through the northern portion of the state of Oregon. May I add that the whole province of New Brunswick is somewhat south of the forty-ninth parallel. Maps such as this, Mr. Speaker, are hanging in the members' rooms, they are in our colleges, in our libraries and schools, and in the offices of our immigration agents.
The maps as distributed .by the Department of Immigration present the same inaccuracies. I do not suppose that the immigrants will study the lines of latitude to check up this strange arrangement, but they will look at the map with a view to seeing at what distance from the north pole a certain province is located. They wish to assure themselves, if possible, of coming to a moderate or temperate climate. It is not sufficient to say that this misrepresentation can be noted and checked up by observing the latitude. I would ask how many of the two hundred and forty-four members of this house-all intelligent observant men-have made this observation. I would ask how many of the general public are likely to do it. I think the answer is obvious.
But here is a still more important point. Many of these maps do not show the latitude, and therefore you cannot check them. Even a geographer would fail to read our geography correctly, as it should 'be read. An officer of the Royal Geographical Society was asked his opinion on these maps, and when I say these maps. I am speaking of those which are incorrect, and they are numerous, although there are maps that are correctly represented, and this officer fully agreed that the projection of a map should be symmetrically placed upon the sheet, so that a curved parallel of latitude would cut eastern and western margins at the same height. He says that on good maps draughtsmen follow this rule, and it is broken only by people who make a map by cutting a portion of a more extensive map and do not trouble to adjust the projection.
Whether that is the true explanation with regard to our Canadian maps I cannot say, but this I do say, that undoubtedly they present a wrong impression and give wrong information to ourselves and to the world, and I draw this matter to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm), the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) and the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke), and ask them to take such action as will avoid in future the perpetuation of the error.

I now come to my second subject, Mr. Speaker, and that is the London treaty, or the London agreement, or the London resolutions of 1S66 and the British North America Act of 1867. One hears frequently of the Quebec resolutions, one hears references beyond number to the British North America Act, but comparatively seldom to the London lesolutions or the London agreement. The Quebec resolutions and the London resolutions are very similar. True, the Quebec resolutions were more fully discussed than the London resolutions. The Quebec resolutions were drawn up not only with the colonies of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia participating, but also the colonies of Prince Edward Island and the colony of Newfoundland. These resolutions were not finally accepted; on the contrary, several of the colonies failed to concur, and therefore there was a conference in London, where representatives from Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia alone met, drew up afresh the resolutions or treaty, and signed the document at the Westminster Palace hotel on December 4, 1866. That is the fundamental document, the basis of confederation. On the London resolutions was framed the British North America Act. This act, I submit, is an enabling act. On what? On the terms of agreement entered into by the four provinces which proposed the confederation.
Now, the British North America Act does not necessarily contain all the provisions in the agreement; as a matter of fact it does not contain them- all, although it contains them very largely. I noticed last session that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his presentation of the Duncan report reminded us of:
The spirit which animated the fathers of confederation in their efforts to construct out of British North America a federal union under a system of government devised to protect the diversified interests of the several provinces and secure efficiency, harmony and permanency in the working of the union.
Where did the Prime Minister obtain that quotation? He obtained it from the second section of the London resolutions. I think we hear far too seldom of the basis of our confederation. I would especially call the attention of the house to one section of the agreement which is not contained in the act, and I should like to place it on Hansard. It is section 66:
The communications with the northwestern territory, and the improvements required for the development of the trade of the great -west with the seaboard, are regarded by this conference as subjects of the highest importance to

I would urge the government in any future issue of the British North America Act fo incorporate the London resolutions. The document should be withdrawn from its dusty quarters, for it is a vital document to-day, and I believe that in the interests of right and justice it should be printed along with the act.

In
rising at this time I should like to say that the people of the province from which I come appreciate the fact that the government in-

tends to turn over to the western provinces their natural resources. I do hope, however, that they will not forget that a large part of our resources have already been taken, and that when the final adjustment is being made that factor of remuneration will be considered, in order to take care of those that have already gone. It is also gratifying to know that the government have taken active and definite steps to complete the Hudson Bay railway to the bay and that in a very short time we will be able to use that line to carry our produce from the prairie provinces to the markets of the world. It is also gratifying to hear of the prosperity of the Dominion generally. The trade figures certainly indicate that business in this country is good. The figures the bankers have given out indicate the same thing. But in spite of the fact that all these things tend toward prosperity, from my observation I am led to believe that the prosperity of our Dominion is not being distributed equally among all the different classes and districts of the Dominion. The agriculturists are the ones Who have laid the foundation for the prosperity of the Dominion. They supply approximately half of our population. The figures that were given in the house some few days ago show that out of an export of $1,218,000,000, grain products were accountable for about $447,000,000. Last year the agricultural production was estimated to be in the neighbourhood of $1,660,000,000, which is a little less than the amount estimated for the previous year. I do not see that any fact has been presented to the house yet to indicate that agriculture is sharing in the prosperity of the country to the extent to which it is entitled. The recent census published in the province of Manitoba shows that in the whole of the province less than two per cent of the farm homes have running water, less than three per cent have electric light and less than 30 per cent have telephones. It seems to me this does not indicate that the people on the prairies are enjoying that prosperity which certain other sections and classes in this country are experiencing. Otherwise they would not be suffering from the lack of such requisites in their homes. Nowadays the telephone is considered indispensable in the home. It certainly is a necessity in the rural districts in the newer portions of the country where doctors, for example, live some distance away from their patients, and where the roads are far from good.
The income tax returns would indicate alsc that people engaged in agriculture are not as prosperous as they might be. Throughout
The Address-Mr. Milne

the whole of Canada only 3,643 farmers are paying income taxes, which serves to show that the vast majority do not earn enough to bring them into the taxable class.
Another thing which indicates, to my mind, that the rural parts of Canada are not as prosperous as they should be is the difficulty in getting immigrants to come and stay. If the conditions in Canada were such that people could go on the land and make a comfortable living there would be no difficulty in securing immigrants. The problem then would be to keep them from entering the country. To-day everybody is crying out for immigration and saying that if we could secure population our problems would be solved. That may be true, but the difficulty seems to be to retain settlers when we get them. In the province of Manitoba between 1921 and 1926 the population increased by a little over 28,000. During the same period the immigration into the province numbered about 30,000 souls sb that not only did the province fail to keep its natural increase, but it lost 2,000 immigrants as well. These figures indicate that conditions are not as good as they might be. If we are to develop our country we must make the pursuit of agriculture more remunerative and profitable, because it is just as true to-day as in the pioneering days that the prosperity of the country depends upon the success of farming. There is no reason in the world why agriculture should not be enjoying a greater measure of prosperity than it actually does. No one has greater faith in the future of this Dominion, or of western Canada, than I have. From the point of view of production there is absolutely nothing wrong with the country nor with its agricultural class, which compares favourably with that of any other country.
One of the big drawbacks to the success of agriculture is the cost of production. The cost of transportation is also high, and that vitally affects the people of the west. Closely related to the cost of production and the cost of transportation is the tariff. The tariff tax is a tax that can be passed on to the consumer. In proof of this may I be permitted to quote from the Retail Trade Review for December, 1927, which makes the following statement:
Indirect taxation, such as customs, excise and sales tax, can be imposed by the Dominion government because manufacturers and producers are supposed to indemnify themselves against the same by passing it on to their customers.
It was proven conclusively, I think, when the duty on automobiles was lowered, that the consuming public were able to buy auto-

mobiles cheaper. I think the same result would follow if the duty were lowered on other goods. Those of us who are engaged in the farming industry believe that if the tariff were reduced on implements of production and the necessities of life we would be able to live more cheaply. According to figures submitted to the tariff board it cost the people of Canada about $19,000,000 to maintain the cotton industry in this country for one year. I do not know what the cost of maintaining the boot and shoe or the woollen industry was, but the amount must have been considerable. Now those who are engaged in pioneering and developing our country, laying the foundations for a better and more prosperous nation, are the people who are called upon to pay these taxes in order that industries may accumulate wealth. In many cases that I know of the children of these taxpayers are very inadequately clad and are unable to go to school except when the weather is mild. Yet these privileged manufacturers come along and ask for higher tariffs, with the result that still greater burdens would be placed upon these poor people whose children, in many cases, are not only poorly clothed but insufficiently fed. They are the people who are being oppressed in order that certain classes of individuals may be able to accumulate wealth.
I do not want to speak at great length but I should like to refer to the duty on cement. Cement is largely used in the rural districts for foundations and floors for farm buildings. In the interest of the conservation of our supply of lumber we ought to encourage the use of cement rather than limit its consumption by the imposition of a tax. If it were for no other reason than that of the conservation of our timber, it would be worth while considering the matter of encouraging the use of cement, but we find a tax of eight cents per 100 pounds imposed on this commodity. I do not know whether this matter has been referred to the tariff advisory board, but we would be almost led to believe the Canada Cement Company, which practically controls the manufacture of cement in this country, is well able to do without a tariff, particularly when we know that during the last few months they split a melon, as the saying is, and presented many of the shareholders with new stock.
Paint is another material which from a conservation standpoint is equally as important as cement. If the buildings, machinery and equipment of the agricultural people are not kept painted, they deteriorate and waste away in a comparatively short time, and

therefore in the interest of conservation the use of paint should be encouraged instead of being hindered by the imposition of a tariff tax. White lead ground in oil bears at the present time a tax of 37J per cent. To my mind this rate is absolutely unreasonable, and further if we have any idea of advertising our country to tourists and immigrants, nothing will attract greater attention and create a better impression than well-painted homes in rural districts and towns throughout Canada. Therefore the government would be well advised, instead of retaining this tax of 37i per cent on white lead, to encourage the use of paint by lowering this tax.
Another tax about which I want to say a few words is the income tax which, in my opinion, is one of the fairest systems of taxation we have, although a definite effort appears to have been launched to eradicate it. In fact, in the same pamphlet to which I referred a short time ago it is declared specifically that they will not let anything stand in the way of their accomplishing the abolition of this tax. I consider this tax is fair because the people who have the income are the people who have to pay it. We hear a great deal about the crop in western Canada this year. It is true that we produced a tremendous quantity of grain, but in spite of that fact there were large areas in the prairies where the crop was far below normal on account of rust, hail, frost and a dozen and one other things that occur at times to take away from us what promises to be a very profitable crop. When we have a tax like the income tax, those people who have been unfortunate in their returns are the people who do not have to pay, while the people who have good returns, either through their work or because of favourable seasons or conditions, are the people who have to pay-
The tariff tax and the sales tax do not take into consideration the prosperity of the individual who pays the tax; they do not take into consideration, as the income tax does, the responsibilities of individuals in regard to their dependents. Generally speaking, the tariff tax and the sales tax have to be paid to a larger extent by people who are developing our natural resources. The people who are making this onslaught on the income tax state in their pamphlet:
Indirect taxation, such as customs, excise and sales tax can be imposed by the Dominion government because manufacturers and producers are supposed to indemnify themselves against the same by passing it on to their customers.
I should like to ask these people who are so determined to abolish the income tax whv the
manufacturers are supposed to be exempt from taxation? What divine right have they that they should not help to bear the burden of the taxation of this country? This same circular makes this statement:
Men and women out of employment, and those who do not earn enough to pay an income tax are indirectly but not directly interested in this subject.
In my opinion they are the people who are vitally interested. According to the latest returns of last year in regard to income tax only about ten per cent of our people pay this direct tax. If they are relieved of the income lax, this means that a burden of 555,500,000 will be thrown on the shoulders of the other ninety per cent of our people who have not sufficient revenues or salaries to be taxable. We are told that the income tax is preventing capital from coming to our country, but any person who has been following the development of Canada will readily realize that this is not the case. Let me ask the government not to make any further reductions in the income tax, but rather that they consider the advisability of taxing the incomes of speculators who speculate on our grain exchanges and stock markets. Those speculators serve no useful purpose; they employ no labour, and I see no reason why such speculation should not be taxed.
I have endeavoured briefly to show that the agricultural community, the people who are laying the foundation of our prosperity, are not receiving their proper share of the prosperity which this country is enjoying, and I suggest that a reduction of the tariff tax on the necessities of life and implements of production will assist those people in ret-ainning what they have worked hard for, and what rightly belongs to them. I humbly suggest that the income tax be not reduced any further, but that consideration be given to the idea of placing a tax on the earnings of speculators who make money in our grain exchanges and bond houses.
