It is also necessary that action be taken for the alleviation of the difficulties of the fishing industry in these provinces. I want to tell hon. gentlemen who do not know just why that is necessary. Some few years ago Nova Scotia was the leading fish-producing province in Canada; to-day British Columbia leads and Nova Scotia is second. But still we have in Nova Scotia some 16,000 fishermen primarily engaged in the industry, 4,000 more who secondarily derive their living from that occupation, and scattered over the whole province thousands more directly affected by it. We have on our shores some of the finest fishing banks in the world, banks to which fishing fleets from far-off Fiance resort. We have a large number of people there who are adaptable to the industry and who love the sea. And yet despite those facts, since 1914 the fishing industry of the province of Nova Scotia has lost 10,000 men, most of whom have gone to the United States to earn their living, because they do not wish to give up their calling, and are pursuing the industry at Gloucester or Boston. Such a state of affairs calls for a remedy. The position in the eastern part of the province is particularly acute. In view of the fact that this commission is sitting and will make its report it is not for me to prescribe a remedy, but it is for me to ask that some steps be taken to improve the conditions down there for the benefit of the people of Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces as a whole.
There is another matter also relating to the fishing industry which I purpose dealing with, and then I am done. I refer to the question I brought to the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) last session. Repeatedly during last session I urged upon him the importance of

The Address-Miss Macphail
having storm warnings broadcast to the fishing fleets. I did that because in August, 1926, two schooners from the Lunenburg fleet went down, taking with them fifty men. Last year, during the progress of his estimates through the house, the minister assured me this would be done in 1927. I regret to say that nothing was done, and in August, 1927, we lost not two but four vessels and eighty men. The disaster is all the more appalling when we stop to think that in some measure this might have been prevented if the assurance given by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had been carried out. The hon. minister is not in his seat now, but I ask him in all sincerity not to wait for the report of the royal commission but to take action during the present session. Let the details be dealt with later on, but let him make a start now in order that such a disaster may not occur in this or in future years so that when the vessels return next autumn there will not be any vacant chairs or aching hearts.

I consider it something of a hardship to follow the very brilliant young member from Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst). We come again to the consideration of the speech from the throne, a speech which I feel sure was evolved in cabinet council, a speech that was written, I feel equally sure, by the first minister, and a speech that has been read to the assembled .commoners and senators by His Excellency the Governor General. In view of the whole matter it is not surprising that when we return to the House of Commons on the day following the formal opening we find the supporters of the administration rising in their places and saying that it is a very good speech. One would hardly under the circumstances expect them to say anything else. However, after reading the speech very carefully I think myself it is an exceedingly clever speech-how adroitly it says nothing at all!
I should not want to fail to congratulate the mover of the address (Mr. Ilsley) on the very excellent speech he made; I most heartily congratulate him. And as for the seconder, my hon. friend from Provencher (Mr. Beau-bien); he is so delightful that one can forgive him much, and when one remembers that he was elected as an independent in 1921 and in 1928 we find him seconding the motion which embodies the scant legislative program of one of the major parties in the house, I feel he needs much forgiveness.

May I ask the hon. member a question? Did the hon. member not vote on previous occasions for addresses 56103-14
in reply to speeches from the throne without having had anything to do with the preparation of them?

Yes, but I did not second them. The hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Mackenzie), who spoke this afternoon, said: "The poor we have with us always." I think he was smugly complacent. He reminded me of an amti-Baptist minister who took as his text, " Beware of divers." The member for Assiniboia lifted the text completely outside the content in order to condone a very iniquitous system. I wonder if he would like to hear some other quotations. I think he would enjoy this: "What mean ye that ye grind the faces of the poor?" "The instruments of the churl are evil." " He deviseth wicked devices to destroy the poor with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right." " He who mocketh the poor reproacheth his maker." " Inasmuch as ye have not done it unto the least of these, ye have not done it unto me." "Depart ye unto outer darkness." I think that might be a word of warning to the Liberal party, that unless they realize that the elimination of poverty of the masses is the work of government, the outer darkness of opposition awaits them.
In the many speeches made on the address in reply to the speech from the throne much has been said about prosperity. I do not consider that adding to the wealth of the wealthy should be called, from a national point of view, prosperity. I think it is as true as when the words were spoken by John Bright to the British government that " the nation of every country dwells in the cottage, and unless the excellence of your statesmanship is impressed there on the feelings and conditions of the people, rely upon it you have yet to learn the art of government." I am glad to admit that conditions in rural Canada and in the homes of the industrial workers are ' slightly better than they were five years ago, but prosperity as it is understood in this house is unknown to our oeople. I had the privilege, and I conside'- it a very great privilege, of visiting last summer very many rural homes in Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and I certainly did not find in those homes the prosperity that I read about in the speech from the throne. I found people struggling to meet debt, and worrying over taxes and meeting the payment of their mortgages. I thought the conditions were particularly bad in the province of Manitoba. I believe it was said by some member this afternoon that they no longer grew grain in Manitoba. Well, I think that was true



The Address-Miss Macpliail
this year. I was thinking that the people who are in that province, when they read the speech from the throne and read the speeches that were made about it, will be amazed to learn that this long looked for prosperity has arrived. I am sure that from the feel of their pocket-book they will not know it has arrived. I visited the area between Sperling and Carman, a very wealthy part of Manitoba. I talked to people who went out there many years ago, relatives of my own, and I was told by them and by their neighbours that not more than three people in that community would be able to pay their taxes this year. I would not call that prosperity. I think one would be safe in saying that not ten per cent of the homes in rural Canada have running water, a bathroom, electric light, and the labour saving devices which the development of power makes possible. I think it is true, and I believe everyone in this house who is familiar with rural conditions will agree, there is too little comfort and beauty in our rural homes. I think too that the people in those rural homes are rebelling against that condition.
I want now to quote very briefly from Means and Methods of Agricultural Education, by Professor Leake, as follows:
Sometimes the drudgery of the farm is endured by the mother uncomplainingly, or even contentedly; but the daughter recoils from it with a growing discontent.
A little later he says:
The great problem, how to keep the boy on the farm, is troubling many, but it would become much less a problem if we could devise ways and means of keeping the girl on the farm. The girls are even more dissatisfied with farm life than the boys, and are leaving in greater numbers. The lessened proportion of women in the country homes of Canada was one of the startling surprises of the last census.
I do not consider that we can boast of our prosperity until that prosperity has reached the homes of the mass of the people. I think it is quite likely that the prosperity that has undoubtedly arrived in certain classes and sections of Canada will continue and will increase, until possibly it reaches boom dimensions, and will be followed by a crash or a long depression comparable to the one out of which we are just emerging. What is the government doing toward determining the cause?
I read with very great interest most, if not all, of the very delightful book which was published and sent to us by the Department of Trade and Commerce, entitled "Diamond Jubilee of the Confederation of Canada: Sixty Years of Canadian Progress." On page 60 of this work I find that the
TMiss Macphail.l
estimated gross agricultural wealth of Canada is $7,508,257,000, and the annual production on that investment is $1,600,000,000. On page 89 of the same volume I find that the total investment in the manufacturing industry is $3,808,282,981 and the annual production on that investment $2,948,545,315. These figures, in brief, mean that agriculture requires a $7 investment for $1 of production, and industry a $3 investment for little better than $2 of production. Under the circumstances we cannot wonder that we have ever with us the problem of rural depopulation. Other figures were given this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), which I need not repeat, showing that while farm lands fell $1 an acre between the years 1925 and 1926, industrial stocks and bonds doubled in value. With these facts clearly before us we can understand why it is that an intelligent and virile people are no longer willing to stay and slave under conditions which are not being remedied and with respect to which no real attempt at remedy is being made. The farmers of Canada are gradually learning that that industry which fails to assume responsibility for marketing its own productions arrives last in this race for the consumer's dollar. They are gradually-I think with increasing rapidity-remedying this by cooperative marketing. However, even though the farmers would market all their products cooperatively there still would rest upon their backs the great burden placed there partly through a bad distribution system of other commodities, and partly as a result of legislation passed by an organized minority for their own benefit.
One of the things to which I refer is the present Bank act. I notice in the W'eekly News of February 3rd, printed in Winnipeg, that the Bank of Nova Scotia made a dividend this year of 164 per cent, which seems a snug little dividend. The Canadian Bank of Commerce made a dividend of 12 per cent, with a bonus of one dollar. It was the same with other banks; evidently they are all making very great profits. Now there is a general feeling in farming districts that our banking system is not all it should be, and that some reform along the line of setting up a bank of issue and rediscount should at once be instituted. The Canadian Council of Agriculture-in April, 1927, passed a resolution to that effect, which I need not trouble the house to read.
Another thing with which the farmers are very familiar is the burden which is placed on them by the customs tariff. I feel it is true that the farmers all over Canada, re-

The Address-Miss Macphail
gardless of the province in which they live, but particularly in certain provinces, are looking to the government this year to bring down a general and very considerable reduction of the customs duties on those things that go to make up the cost of living, on the necessities of life and on the implements of production. I see no excuse which will enable the government to escape this time. I am sure that if there is any, they will find it, but it does not appear to me that there is any way of escape for them. They used to say they did not know just what to reduce, because of the danger of hurting some very necessary industry; but with the sittings held by the tariff board, the very excellent work that is being done by that body and the great quantities of data now before the government on this question, I cannot for the life of me see how they are going to say that they cannot now scientifically reduce the tariff. Of course they have a majority and that to me is not a hopeful thing.
I want to speak of another njatter. I am pleased to know that Canada has a nonpermanent seat on the council of the League of Nations. I think we are all very glad of that. I think we feel that Canada can do a very great work for humanity by being on that council. I believe the term is three years, although I am not quite sure as to the period. I hope that Canada, as an autonomous nation, will take a strong stand on the principle of arbitration, and will express her willingness to sign arbitration treaties with as many countries as are willing to sign them with us.	There is no reason
in the world why we should not do it. I believe it would be appreciated by other dominions and indeed by a large section of the people in the motherland.
I noticed, and I daresay all the other members of the house noticed, a very interesting editorial published in the Citizen this morning with reference to the International Joint Commission. It pointed out that for sixteen years Canada and the United States have had a board of arbitration working, and working with very great success, composed of three members from each country and that when it sits in this country a Canadian presides and when it sits in the other country an American presides. It is an interesting fact that all the questions that have been referred to this commission have been settled by the unanimous consent of the board in a way that has been pleasing to both countries. This is something of which both Canada and the United States ought to be veipr proud, and something that, without boasting, we could make known to the world. One feels that a 56103-144
rather tense atmosphere has recently arisen between the United States and Great Britain, and this is something that we all very deeply regret. I quite understand that I am a very simple soul, but I can see no reason why a commission similar to this cannot be set up between Great Britain and the United States.
Canada through her representative on the League of Nations should take a very strong stand against the international trade in arms and armaments. Somebody ought certainly to take a stand and there is no reason Why we should not do so. I find in private life that people who stand around waiting for somebody else to give them a lead are not of very great consequence. We should have initiative both as individuals and as a country, and through our representative on the League of Nations we should take a strong stand on questions on which we feel strongly. That this would be acceptable to at least some people and, I believe, to a large number of people in the motherland is quite clear from this quotation from Arthur Ponsonby's book, Now Is The Time, at page 82. He says:
Any disposition on the part of our dominions to refuse to join in these wars of European origin will be all to the good. The dead weight of a reasonable pacifism from that quarter might have a moderating effect on the home government.
He goes on to say things even more startling than that, but I will not take the time to read them to the house. I should like to draw the attention of our government to the fact i that now in the quiet and sanity of peace nine there are some things which we could do to show the world that we have definitely turned our backs upon old methods of settling international disputes. One is that the government should have full control of the manufacture of munitions. I see no reason why the manufacture of munitions which are designed to bring about the death of human beings should be in- the hands of private individuals who can and who have used this power for private gain. Let us now make a law stating that, if the worst came to the worst at any time in the future and we must face war, all property will be administered by the state; that is, there would be a complete conscription of wealth. I feel this would have a moderating influence upon certain elements in Canada.
In this connection, while this may seem presumption on my part, I urge the government completely to divorce aviation, which is rapidly developing along civil lines, from the military department, and not only from the military department but from military person-ilities. It would seem reasonable that in the

The Address-Miss Macphail
lear future we should form a department of iransportation which would include aviation dong with railways and canals, and national highways, if we should ever have such a thing.
I should like respectfully to ask the government when they intend to change the administration of the penitentiaries so that prisoners will be given as much work as they can comfortably do in a day and will be paid a decent wage for that work. We have heard a great deal about this; the house carried the resolution some time ago-let us have the legislation. We should go further than this, because it is only one little step, as we so often say in this house, in the right direction. A real study should be made of crime; we are all coming to the place where we admit that crime is caused by ignorance, poverty, lack of culture, lack of happiness. There are many things about the prisoners that need study besides the one that I have mentioned. In our whole system of taking care of prisoners we should look to the good that we can do to the prisoner while he is detained by the state, making him feel that the state is fair to him. That is why I want him to be paid a decent wage for his work, from which wage, of course, his keep must be deducted. We must never forget, too, that the family of the prisoner possibly suffers more than the prisoner himself, and when the prisoner comes out, there should be, shall we say, a fatherly hand of the government to guide that man into civil life, to re-establish him. So many of them when they first get out try for a few days or weeks to go in what we call a straight way, and not being able to do that they very soon revert to crime. Much could be done by the state to make these things better for the men and women
My stand on immigration is exactly what it has always been since I came to this house, and that is that if we would turn our minds to remedying conditions in the primary industries in Canada and do less talking and less spending of money bringing in state-aided immigrants to this country, we would be getting further on the road we all want to travel. We should look to the quality rather than to the quantity of immigration that comes to Canada. Any immigration policy worthy of the name should hold sacred, first, the ultimate good of Canada and, second, the good of the immigrant. Sometimes I think the good of the immigrant is not very much considered, although I may be wrong in that. Particular care should be taken to guard immigrants who do not speak the English language against fraud on the part of our loyal citizens when those immigrants [Miss Macohail.l
first arrive in this country. I have heard some amazing stories about what sometimes happens to non-English speaking immigrants when they first arrive in Canada and especially when they have some money. If we are going to have a stimulated immigration policy we might as well face the fact now as at any other time that we must inaugurate a policy of industrial or unemployment insurance. We simply cannot bring thousands of prospective settlers to this country letting them think we are going to take care of them and then not doing it when sickness or lack of employment or lack of warm clothing in our Canadian winter comes upon them. We must make up our minds one way or the other.
A week ago I was in the city of Windsor. I passed the factory of the General Motors, which was to be opened in a day or two but was not open at that time, and I saw actually hundreds of men standing in line waiting to see if they could get a job. I was with the librarian as we had come down to look through the library, and the reading rooms were not only comfortably filled but actually packed with men whom this tenderhearted woman said she could not turn out into the cold. There they were day after day as it was one warm place in the city of Windsor.
I hope during this session something will be done towards enabling married women to establish a legal domicile. This question has been debated in this house and as it was introduced by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) who, I believe, is a stepson of the government, I see no reason why they should not father his bill. The Canadian Council of Agriculture deals with the matter in this way:
Whereas the Canadian Council of Agriculture has for the past number of years passed resolutions asking that the inequality in our law as between men and women in the matter of domicile be removed.
Therefore be it resolved that we reaffirm our position on this question, and urge upon the Dominion government the enactment into law of Bill 111 introduced by W. J. Ward, M.P., Dauphin, enabling a woman for purposes of judicial separation or divorce to establish a legal domicile of her own.
I hope the government will look with very kind eyes upon this matter.
In closing, let me say that I am a member of an independent group. I am not interested in party politics; I am not interested in parties, although I must say in all fairness that I am very much interested in the people who compose the parties. I am at all times ready, and indeed anxious, to support legislation which to my mind is beneficial to the

The Address-Mr. Jenkins
constituency I have the honour to represent -I believe that is the correct form-and to the country as a whole. I want to help with legislation, but I can only help with it if the legislation is pleasing to the people who sent me here, and knowing what I do from six years in public life I fear that the legislative program of this session will not weary us too much. I do not believe that when you have a stable government-one with a very comfortable majority, you get good government. I may be wrong; I sometimes am, but I think not in this case, and so, having inpower a stable government, one with a very comfortable majority, a majority that unfortunately has been added to by men who should have known better, I do not see how we can expect a legislative program that will be pleasing to our constituencies. But at least we are here to get for the common people of Canada the best that we can, and I am here sitting ready to be pleasantly surprised by the government.

Mr. Speaker, permit me first of all to congratulate the mover (Mr. Ilsley) and the seconder (Mr. Beaubien) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and at the same time to extend my sincere congratulations to the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) who has been elected to such a high and honourable position.
The speech from the throne has in general met with the approval of the members of this house.
There were, however, those who voiced disappointment that it did not go far enough, but we presume, Mr. Speaker, that the budget which will be brought down later on by the Finance minister (Mr. Robb) will supplement for our friends what the speech apparently lacked for them. From what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said, we can safely surmise that some pleasing revelations will be made, and from our experience of the last two years we may assume that our genial Finance minister will go even a little further than we hope or expect.
The speech, first of all, bears testimony to the fact that generally speaking conditions are good in Canada. I need not enlarge upon this phase of the subject, because it has been carefully covered by the speech of the Prime Minister and others who followed him; but I would just like to quote a few words from an address delivered by the vice-president and general manager of the Dominion bank at their annual meeting a few days ago:
This is the land of opportunity. Those Canadians whose early recollections go back to
confederation days cannot, when comparing the conditions then and now', but feel satisfaction and pride in the progress that, in spite of periodical setbacks, remains as the net result of sixty years. We can now look forward with confidence to a reasonable measure of fulfilment of a famous prophecy: "The Twentieth Century will belong to Canada."
A few words pertaining to conditions in my own province may not be amiss, Mr. Speaker. As a general rule we do not have any violent swings either upwards or downwards; things run along in a very even way. We have no great wealth and very little poverty. Our people as a rule are prosperous, and are willing to work and do their fair share in the upbuilding of Canada. In his report for this year, president R. L. Cotton of the Charlottetown board of trade says:
So far as our city (Charlottetown) and our province is concerned, the year has been one of more than usual progress and prosperity.
The fox business was especially good, and high prices prevailed not only for live foxes, but for pelts as well. This brought a very large amount of outside money into the province which tended to stimulate and help along business in every line. I think it is safe to say, however, Mr. Speaker, that as far as farm conditions are concerned, 1927 would hardly equal 1926 owing to the fact that the prices of many commodities were rather low, notably those of pork and potatoes. We have had a very fair crop of the latter commodity, *and thousands of bushels were exported to -the southern United States for seed purposes, but the price prevailing was rather low and would not give the farmers a very great leeway over cost of production. I am thankful to say, Mr. Speaker, that the warehouse facilities provided at Charlottetown, Summerside, and Georgetown for the handling of this particular commodity are of great assistance to our people and we deeply appreciate the consideration of this government in relation thereto. Mr. Boulter, secretary of the potato growers' association in an interview with the press a few days ago stated:
The volume of business during the fall season ending December 31, 1927 far exceeded that of any entire year of business since the association was organized. Considerably over one million bushels of potatoes were handled and twenty thousand bushels of turnips. The open fall aided greatly in the movements by water, the association having loaded in all sixteen steamers which would average over fifty thousand bushels per steamer. Three ports were used in loading, Summerside, Charlottetown and Georgetown. Without these added warehouses it would have been impossible to have moved such a large quantity by water. The Georgetown warehouse proved of exceptional value, as the seed shipped from this
The Address-Mr. Jenkins

port was for points south, whose growers would not under any consideration accept early shipments of seed. The fact, therefore, that the association was able to make these late shipments through Georgetown not only held the territory which they opened up last year, but allowed them to reach more distant markets, going even into Tennessee and Alabama, and seed shipments by water next year will in all probability be made as far as New Orleans in the gulf of Mexico. Many of our potatoes were also exported to Cuba and Canadian markets as well.
The sixtieth anniversay of confederation was duly celebrated in our province in common with other parts of the Dominion. We have a loyal and patriotic people and the celebrations were of a very high character
The speech from the throne refers to immigration. So far as Prince Edward Island is concerned we can only assimilate a limited number and they should be of a class of farmers who have some means at their command and who can go on the land, pay for it, purchase agricultural implements and not be hampered by debts of any kind. People of this sort are bound to make good, provided they are willing to work. We may also have a limited demand for farm help, but what we need above all else is to keep our own people on the farms. In this connection I Should like to quote from the speech made in this debate the other day by the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette), who made a speech that is well worth reading. At page 177 of Hansard he says:
Let me go a step further. I do not believe we shall need so many immigrants, and I am sure we will not lose our population to such a great extent, if the government will do something to see that young Canadians are offered some inducement to go on the farms and stay there. As you know, the bright lights of the cities, with 'their theatres, dance halls and so on, are wonderfully attractive even to the urban population, so it is no wonder that the young people are attracted from the country.
I Should also like to quote again from the address made by the vice-president and general manager of the Dominion bank at their annual meeting. He said:
With respect to the important question of immigration, there is some encouragement in the fact that 1927 figures were the largest since 1913, and various colonization enterprises are proving successful, but the number of settlers is still very far short of our needs and capacity, and a more energetic policy by our government is required to revive the prewar flow of newcomers. The shift of population from the country to the city in the older provinces is a constant and partly inevitable condition brought about because the increased use of machinery in agriculture releases man-power, and also by the concentration of mass-production industry in the large labour centres. An additional, and a regretfMr. Jenkins.l
able, cause is that many young men born on the farm seem not to care for the life. Out-government should do everything possible to encourage our people to stay on the land.
One of the hon. members who spoke in this debate tonight referred to the fact that the young ladies were also dissatisfied. Our government should do everything possible to encourage the people to stay on the land. Some encouragement should be given to the sons of farmers to settle on the land, and if a scheme were devised whereby they would [DOT]receive assistance along lines such as that of the soldier settlement scheme with a loan of money and easy payments thereon, it would I believe be a great deal better than making experiments with people who are not suitable to our country, and who will not make good. We have had quite a number of immigrants coming into our province in past years. Some of them have succeeded, and others unacquainted with farms conditions made a failure with us, the same as they would anywhere else.
At a meeting in Charlottetown the other day .one of these gentlemen who came out from the old country stated in an address before the Rotary Club that he had an easier time on Prince Edward Island than he ever had at home. He was able to put a few dollars in the bank, something he could not do in the old land. This gentleman stated that it was detrimental to both countries to bring out unsuitable men, and when I see in Prince Edward Island, he said, big farms not half cultivated, I am convinced we should have more settlers of the right sort. He said:
Coming to the Island is like coming home. The scenery is much the same. Loneliness and homesickness are not felt so much here. The people are kind and sociable. There are opportunities on the island for practical farmers with a little capital. In the old country many are just making a bare living on small holdings. The taxes and rent are a great handicap. For instance on 30 acres of land a man pays $450 per year rent and $100 in taxes.
This amount seems rather exorbitant, nevertheless it is what this report states:
The farmers in the old country must be convinced first that it is to their advantage to immigrate. They will hesitate before selling their stock and home unless they know exactly how they will fare in Canada. The immigrant agent must tell them the plain truth about conditions here, tell them what the land is like, and what it will cost.
In the old country the farmers work from 12 to 16 hours per day. There is no need of it here. He had an easier time than ever he had at home, and was able to put a few dollars in the bank, something he couldn't do there.

The Address-Mr. Jenkins
While here there is good land, with a good and easy market for the produce, handy to neighbours, with horses and barns ready for the settler and with land already cleared, there is an impression in the old country that Canada is a wild country overrun by wild beasts.
The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) has just emphasized what has so often been emphasized in this house, that what we need is quality and not quantity.
The speech from the throne also refers to the fact that so far as the maritime provinces are concerned, the increases in subsidy recommended by the Duncan report" will be continued this year. We firmly believe however, Mr. Speaker, when our claims are fully considered, that as a province we should receive much greater consideration in regard to subsidy allowance than we are receiving at the present time.
If the Prime Minister and his government in April 1926 had done nothing else but appoint the royal commission on maritime rights, they would be entitled to the gratitude not only of the maritimes, but of the whole Dominion; for a chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and our country between the two oceans is indissolubly bound together; otherwise the spirit and meaning of confederation could not possibly be carried out. It has been said that the maritimes believe that confederation must be held together by sentiment, by the strong influence of a truly national spirit, assured and supported by an equitable federal agreement. It is contended that if Canada is to become a nation imbued with a truly national spirit selfish sectionalism so often displayed in the past must disappear.
It was to bring about such a spirit, and at the same time see to it that the Atlantic provinces were placed on a level with other parts of Canada with respect to trade and commerce, transportation and all that enters into progress and development, that the Prime Minister and his cabinet conceived and carried out the idea of the royal commission on maritime rights. If the report of that commission will do nothing more than educate the people of the maritimes and the other provinces of Canada on this vital and all absorbing problem, then it will have done much in the way of benefiting trade and commerce and more closely cementing the bonds of confederation.
As was believed by all who understood the people down by the sea, the Duncan report confirmed the view that the faith and interest of the maritime provinces in the general prosperity of Canada are' beyond question-* for our people adhere sincerely to the opinion that the solution of the problems of our own
and the other two provinces by the sea, should and can be found within the policies of this great Dominion.
The terms and conditions upon which Prince Edward Island entered confederation in 1873 contain the following significant provision: Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mail and passengers to be established, and maintained, between the island and the mainland of the Dominion, winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial railway and the railway system of the Dominion.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is well known, for it has often been stated and reiterated on the floor of the House of Commons, that this, the chief provision of the confederation pact so far as the island is concerned, has never been implemented according to the letter of the bond. So far as communication is concerned I believe that the government will carry into effect the recommendation of the Duncan commission, and provide another car ferry. Three years ago on the floor of this house I advocated that this matter should be dealt with, and I understand that the government for some time, through the Department of Railways, has been gathering information and making preparations for this desired improvement. We are sincerely hopeful that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) will see fit to place, if not in the main estimates at least in the supplementary ones, an appropriation for this much needed work. These facilities will have a tendency to keep our people in the province and will give us an added sense of security, more especially so far as trade and commerce is concerned; because, Mr. Speaker, you may produce the finest products in the world, but if you cannot market them in the best condition and when the demand requires, they will certainly depreciate in value. Before our car ferry service was installed, it has been proved from statistics that our farmers realized a little more then 50 per cent of the value in other parts of Canada for their produce, owing to the fact that they were compelled to ship everything out and glut the market before close of navigation. To-day we can ship out practically at all seasons, and with the fine quality we produce we are able to command excellent prices for our products, in the markets not only of Canada but the United States as well.
The fisheries of our province are worth annually well over a million dollars. The marketed value for the past few years has been: 1924, $1,201,772; 1925, $1,598,119; 1926, $1,358,934. The figures for 1927 are not yet available. Although the catch was about the
The Address-Mr. Jenkins

same as that of the preceding year, its value will be somewhat less owing to the lower prices prevailing. The lobster catch in 1927 was 62,233 cwts. as compared with 66,298 cwts. in 1926. This very important fishery is hardly holding its own. Prince Edward Island has adjacent to it fishing areas of great producing capacity, and there is no question that if better prices could be obtained such fisheries as those of cod, haddock, herring and mackerel could be largely developed.
The oysters of Prince Edward Island are, in quality, second to none, but the fishery has now dwindled to about a quarter of its proportions of years gone by. For instance, in 1901 the catch was 24,972 barrels, whereas in 1927 it was only 4,064 barrels. There is no question but that the beds were fished too heavily in years gone by, but the main cause for the reduction is that several years ago a disease broke out amongst the oysters in the far-famed Malpeque bay area, which resulted in the death of the oysters on all the beds in the bay proper. Oyster farming has proved itself just as feasible as land fanning, and, where conditions are favourable, it has shown itself to be much more remunerative. The production of oysters under natural conditions about the island should leave no room for doubt that oyster culture would be successful there, if properly conducted. Keeping in view the areas that are regarded as suitable for oyster culture, there are the best of reasons for believing that, if properly conducted, the oyster fishery of Prince Edward Island could be made many times more valuable than it ever was, or is at the present time.
The situation is complicated by a division of jurisdiction, as while the regulation of this fishery comes under federal jurisdiction, the leasing of areas suitable for oyster farming is a provincial matter. It is understood that negotiations have been in process with the provinces for some time, whereby the full jurisdiction will be placed in the hands of the federal government, which has intimated that it is prepared to do what may be regarded as necessary to bring about an industry in oyster culture and cultivation, if such transfer of jurisdiction is made. I sincerely trust that this matter will receive the immediate consideration of the federal and our own provincial authorities.
As regards the fishing industry, I want to say how deeply indebted we are to this government for the appointment of the fisheries commission. The fishermen deserve every consideration from this house; they work hard and their hours are long and arduous. I do hope that when the report of this commission

is submitted to parliament it will be given the most favourable consideration, because it is my sincere belief that our fishermen as a class have not in the past received that treatment which they should have been given.
In connection with our transportation problems, it is pleasing to note that the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) in cooperation with the Department of National Defence has placed in operation a weekly air mail service between Moncton and the Magdalen Islands. This service passes right over Charlottetown, and I think it would be a fine thing if the postmaster general could arrange to have any delayed mails which may be held at Moncton delivered promptly at Charlottetown. We are looking forward at no distant date to the establishment of a daily air service between the island and the mainland. This no doubt will assist the people of my province in some of their difficulties.
Our province never had crown lands in the general meaning of the term. Its lands were held by proprietors who had received them in grant from the British crown, and who leased them to settlers. In 1853 the legislature of the then colony empowered the government to purchase the land from the proprietors and to sell it outright to settlers. Before confederation approximately three-fifths of the land was bought from the proprietors either by the government, which paid for it out of current revenue, or by the tenants themselves.
One of the terms and conditions of our province's entry into confederation was:
That as the government of Prince Edward Island holds no land from the crown, and consequently enjoys no revenue from that source for the construction and maintenance of local works, the Dominion government shall pay by half-yearly instalments, in advance, to the government of Prince Edward Island, forty-five thousand dollars per annum, less interest at five per centum per annum upon any sum not exceeding eight hundred thousand dollars, which the Dominion government may advance to the Prince Edward Island government for the purchase of lands now held by large proprietors.
Advances were drawn by the province against the sum allowed in the foregoing provision to nearly the full extent for the purpose of buying out the remaining absentee proprietorships and transferring the lands to their own settlers. In the nature of things, the transaction was a costly one to the province, from the point of view both of its administrative expense and of loss of interest as well. There was, in addition, a net cash loss of $190,000 on the principal outlay. The government submitted to the Duncan commission a detailed claim, showing a very considerable gross loss on these land transactions.

The Address-Mr. Jenkins
In a book called Confederation Documents I find that a conference was held on December 4, 1866, at Westminster Palace Hotel, London, England, of delegations from the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. This conference was held for the purpose of arranging terms of union of those provinces. There were six members representing Canada, headed by Sir John A. Macdonald, Attorney General and Minister of Militia of Canada, five representatives from Nova Scotia and five from New Brunswick. At this conference the following resolution was passed and ordered to be forwarded to the Right Hon. the Earl of Carnarvon, Secretary of State for the Colonies:
That in case the colony of Prince Edward Island should hereafter desire to join the confederation of Canada, this conference recommends that the government of the confederation should deal with the question of compensation for the proprietary rights in the island in the most liberal spirit possible.
This resolution, Mr. Speaker, only goes to show that it was the desire of ill parties to deal with our province in a fair and equitable way, and as the resolution states, in a most liberal spirit. That, I take it, is the spirit of confederation, and I firmly believe the people of this Dominion are willing to treat our province in this way.
We are sincerely grateful for the many recommendations made in the Duncan report which have been carried out. My hon. friend said that very few of these recommendations had been implemented. He is wrong. There are a few things which will have to be attended to in order to implement that report in full; two of these I have already alluded to, nomely, the increase in subsidy and the improvement of the oar ferry service between Borden and Cape Tormentine, but we have yet a great deal to be accomplished so far as our railway facilities are concerned.
From the different parts of the province our people are crying out for better railway accommodation and also for branch lines in order that they may market their produce in a better and more efficient way. Our province is the most densly populated in the Dominion, ijnd for this reason the transportation facilities should be increased. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Sinclair) and myself have already presented a petition to the governor in council with regard to these branch lines, and I am hopeful that we shall receive some consideration. I understand that the member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) needs branch lines in his county, and no doubt he will later on present his case. In connection with a request for one of these branch lines, I have received a letter showing the amount
of tonnage that might be expected on a section of the proposed railway. With the permission of the house I desire to put on Hansard this letter, which is signed by reliable men. It reads as follows:

When the railway budget is before this house we shall take the opportunity of asking for a statement from the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) regarding proposed railway improvements. I take the liberty of giving him this notice so that he may be prepared. On" one branch of the railway system, known as the Murray Harbor line, we are running on the old narrow gauge, and this is a matter which should receive the serious attention of the railway authorities. The rolling stock is antiquated and out of date, and goods shipped on this particular line must in many cases be rehandled at Charlottetown, thus adding extra expense and damage to goods as well. I plead with the railway management that this matter shall receive immediate and careful consideration and, more than that, immediate action.
When all 1he recommendations, Mr. Speaker, of the Duncan report are carried into effect, no longer shall maritime rights be before the country. All that our people have asked for is justice under the confederation pact. This independent commission has acted with wisdom and discretion, and I am satisfied that the results will meet with the
The Address-Mr. Cowan

approval of all. I believe the spirit of fair play and justice which actuates hon. members of this house will see to it that the people of my province shall equally enjoy all rights and advantages along with the rest of Canada, and so, Mr. Speaker, we shall have a happy, contented and prosperous people.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. J. COWAN (Port Arthur-Thun-der Bay):
speechtext:
I desire, Mr. Speaker, to add my voice to those of other members who have joined in felicitating the mover (Mr. Ilsley) and the seconder (Mr. Beaubien) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. This is the first time I have heard a speech moved and seconded in this house and I take it for granted that the words of commendation which have been uttered by hon. members are well merited.
At the outset I wish to make a few observations concerning a matter referred to in the speech of the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette) regarding the Transcontinental railway. In the constituency I have the honour to represent there are several organized municipalities similar to those referred to by the hon. member. They do not obtain any taxes on property owned and operated by the national railways, and that gives rise to a peculiar situation. Some municipalities do collect from that railway which, prior to the formation of the Canadian National system, was knovra as the Canadian Northern. The town of Sioux Lookout, which is a thriving town in northern Ontario very close to' the present development in the Red lake and Woman lake mining areas, is not. in the fortunate position of obtaining taxation from that railway, and I desire to join with the member for North Timiskaming in urging upon the government, and particularly upon the Minister of Railways, that they take up this question at once and see to it that justice is done these organized municipalities.
In the speech from the throne reference is made to the successful inauguration of an air mail service between Rimouski and Montreal. Again I would suggest that, if that service is operating to the satisfaction of the department, an air service be established in the northern part of northern Ontario where it is impossible to secure railway communication and where the people, especially in the mining areas, are dependent for success and for the speedy transaction of business upon the early receipt and departure of mails.
There is one other matter not referred to in the speech from the throne but which the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie

King) referred to and that was the development and construction of the international waterway, a subject by the way which appeals strongly to the people of the community in which I reside, namely, Port Arthur. It is particularly true that the towns and communities along the international waterway are interested in the development, and in the limited time at my disposal at this time I do not intend to go into any lengthy dissertation on that particular subject. Later during the session I hope to have an opportunity of saying a few words in that connection, but at this time I simply desire to say to the government that I think I represent the aspirations and thought of the people of the country when I urge that there should be no undue delay in pushing forward the construction of the international waterway. It will facilitate the movement of grain and other produce and traffic from the west, and now that the Welland canal is near completion-I understand it will be ready for use in 1931-every effort should be made to advance by all possible means the construction of the main portions of the international St. Lawrence waterway.
It is my purpose to-night to bring to the attention of the house a matter which I suggest has been entirely neglected by the government for the last six or seven years, a matter which pertains particularly to the district I represent. I think moreover it is of interest to the whole of Canada-I refer to what is known in our particular locality as the iron ore industry. I do not have to elaborate on this question at any great length, because I am sure that those who are readers of the newspapers and are interested in the development of that broad stretch of country between the east and the west of Canada are aware of the great development that is taking place there, and it is our hope that the iron ore industry in particular will receive attention from the government. The great area to which I refer, extending as you will notice from the Rouyn district of Quebec right through the Pre-cambrian shield of northern Ontario and through Manitoba to Saskatchewan, is the most highly mineralized area in the world. Geologists tell us that in that formation is found all the great mines that are in existence to-day. There is the Mysore in India, the Rand in South Africa; and that same formation is found in Norway and Sweden and in the northern part of Germany. Of this great Pre-eambrian shield ninety-five per cent is in Canada and five per cent in the United States, and in that five per cent in the United States we find the great Mesaba

The Address-Mr. Cowan
range upon which to-day the prosperity of the United States in regard to steel production depends. Very little of that whole ninety-five per cent of the Pre-cambrian shield that exists in Ontario has been prospected. Surely if the proper means were taken by the government that whole area could be developed and we should find within it unlimited wealth.
I subscribe to the words uttered by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson) when he stated that he hoped that in northern Manitoba would be found a continuation of the same mineralized area that we have in northern Ontario and northern Quebec. Apparently there is some ground for his belief that such is the case, for you will notice that in the last year or so the development of the Flin Flon on the boundary of Saskatchewan and Manitoba has been one of the greatest discoveries of this age.
I sincerely hope that the area to which the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre refers will enjoy equal prosperity with that of northern Ontario. Why do I bring this subject before the house? It is for this reason: There has been development in the past in this particular area. Up to 1921, of the iron ore smelted in Canada nearly thirty-three per cent was obtained from Canadian mines and smelted in Canadian furnaces, the balance coming from the United States. To-day there is not a single once of Canadian ore mined or smelted in Canada. Every ton that is brought in comes either from Newfoundland, which now provides at least thirty-three per cent of it, or from the United States. Surely the proposition does not require argument that we should develop our own resources. There is no doubt the mineral is there. There is no doubt that it should be developed.
You can apply the same reasoning to the pulp and timber resources of that north country. One thing which has helped Canada in regard to the balance of trade is the development of the pulp and timber resources of Ontario, and if the mineralized area of northern Ontario were developed to the same extent it should aid us in presenting a more favourable balance. The remedy I intend to suggest is not a new one; it has been adopted in the past. The government of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier introduced legislation in this regard in 1896. I heard one hon gentleman to-day state that Sir Wilfrid Laurier suggested that the twentieth century belonged to Canada. I think he must have had an idea that the Conservative party would be the leaders of the government during that century, and if they had been I have
no doubt that this industry would not have been allowed to languish as it has, particularly during the last six years.
In 1898 a bounty of S3 per ton was made payable on pig iron, puddled bars, steel billets and ingots, and also a bounty of $2 per ton on pig iron produced from foreign ores. This did stimulate the industry, and progress was rapid. In 1904 the bounty was made applicable to the production of rolled round wire rods and certain other manufacturers of steel, and in 1909 to pig iron and steel produced by the electric process. From time to time the amount of the bounty was varied, and in 1912, the sum of 817,000,000 having been paid out in establishing the industry, all forms of direct government assistance were withdrawn. This ought to convince our friends to the right of the Speaker that if in that period of time to which I refer there was prosperity, surely the enactment of legislation now providing a bounty would make us more prosperous. In 1921 the last iron ore was produced in Canada and there had been paid out in bounties up to 1911 the sum of $17,000,000. For the next seven or eight years no further bounty was paid, and by 1921- which synchronized I think with the elections of that year-not another ton of iron ore was being produced in Canada. From that day to this there have been brought into Canada annually 750,000 tons of ore, one-third from Newfoundland and the other two-thirds from the United States. As I said a moment ago, it is a self-evident proposition that our own resources should be developed and manufactured into the finished article in Canada by Canadian labour.
The following companies have furnaces in Canada:
The Algoma Steel Corporation, Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario.-Has four furnaces with a combined capacity of 1,450 tons of pig iron daily. During 1922 they operated one furnace in January, two for the next seven months, and one only for the remainder of the year. This furnace is worked to only one-fourth of its capacity. It is situated within a few miles of where the greatest deposits of iron are found.
The Atikokan Iron Company, Port Arthur, Ontario.-Has one furnace of 175 tons daily capacity, which has been idle since 1911.
Canadian Furnace Company, Port Colbome, Ontario.-Has one furnace of 325 tons daily capacity.
Midland Iron & Steel Company, Midland, Ontario.-Has one furnace with capacity of 120 tons per day. Idle since October, 1919-
The Address-Mr. Cowan

Parry Sound Iron Company, Midland, Ontario.-Has a furnace at Parry Sound of 90 tons daily capacity. Idle since October, 1919.
Standard Iron Company, Deseronto, Ontario.-Has one furnace of 60 tons daily capacity, that has not been in operation since June, 1919.
Steel Company of Canada, Hamilton, Ontario.-Is operating two furnaces with combined capacity of 750 tons daily.
The Canadian Steel Corporation.-Has erected at Ojibway, near Windsor, two large blast furnaces, but has not yet operated them.
As I have pointed out, millions of dollars have been invested in these furnaces, and with the cessation of the bounty formerly voted all of them are idle except one. Surely that is a striking statement to make in regard to an industry which should be one of the basic industries of Canada, and one which is so fraught with the possibilities of making this country one of the great manufacturing centres of the world. Because after all, steel and iron are basic products in the manufacturing industry in every country. The iron and steel industry is one which has helped to make the United States so exceedingly prosperous, and if proper methods were applied here, I have no doubt the same result would be secured in Canada.
Now the remedy which has been suggested for the present condition of affairs was suggested by the commission appointed by the Drury government in 1923. That commission brought in an unanimous finding and reported to the Ontario government in favour of providing a bounty on the iron ore mined and put through the furnaces of Ontario. They said, moreover, that at least one-half of the bounty should be paid by the Dominion, seeing that the Dominion would obtain direct benefit from the re-establishment of the industry. May I say that the Ontario legislative assembly has already put in force-I think they did it two years ago-legislation implementing that report, so that the province stands ready to-day to assist this government if it will only provide the other half of the bounty. It may be argued by those who are not interested in the development of our iron ores, or in the metal industries of Canada that such a bounty should not be granted. May I point out that bounties are already granted under various names and disguises? For instance, experimental farms are established at government expense to aid agriculture. Thoroughbred stock is distributed at the government's expense with the same object in view. To perpetuate the fishing industry hatcheries are maintained by

the government at various points, and the credit of the province of Ontario is pledged for the production of Cheap power. These are all bonuses of one kind or another, and I claim that the iron ore industry should be put upon the same basis.
I was very much struck with the remarks of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) in favour of granting assistance for the transportation of Alberta coal. That is just as much of a bonus as the assistance I am urging in aid of iron ore. The hon. member is asking that Alberta coal be transported at a reduced rate. Such assistance as that should not be considered as anything else than a bonus. I have every sympathy for the eloquent member for Bow River in the address which he made. I believe that his appeal is sound, but I maintain that the claim I am now advancing is equally entitled to consideration. I do not think it is necessary to labour the subject any further. Where formerly hundreds of tons of iron ore were mined in this country, not an ounce is now * brought forth. That ^atement in itself should be sufficient to commend the proposal I am making to the favourable attention of the government.
What benefits would result if the proposed aid were granted? In the first place the area to which I refer is sparsely settled; it extends from North Bay to the Manitoba boundary. Everyone knows that where a mining camp is established a town springs up immediately. Hon. members who have visited northern Ontario must have been struck with the Hollinger mine, which employs 3,000 people. That means support for at least 10,000 men, women and children. If only one mine were developed it would amply repay the government for the expenditure involved. It would create a more favourable balance of trade, because we are to-day importing from the United States and Newfoundland from two to three million dollars of iron ore per annum. Moreover the revival of this industry would provide employment for our own people. We have heard a great deal in regard to immigration. I am not so much concerned about immigration, although we need an increase of population. What I am interested in is the conservation of our population, the providing of an opportunity in Canada for the employment of our own people, retaining in this country those people who to-day are going to the United States on account of the pay cheque there being larger and more likely to be realized.
So I say that in this northern country mining must play no small part in the general

The Address-Mr. Heaps
plan of Canada's development. Providing our own iron ore from our own resources is a splendid objective in itself, but even that may be considered only as a means to an end if we can colonize and develop our vast northern territory. In doing so we shall assist in solving our railway problem and in bridging the gap which exists between eastern and western Canada. Hon. members know very well that by developing our iron mines the farming community will be greatly aided because it will establish a profitable market for the commodities produced on the farm, to say nothing of the all-round development to which it will conduce. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this is a matter which in all fairness the government should seriously consider in order that they may re-enact the legislation which existed from 1896 to 1921.

Two-thirds of the group to which I have the honour to belong have already spoken in this debate, and the only excuse I have for rising at this particular time is the fact that we represent a much larger number of electors than might be inferred from our numerical strength in this house. In the last federal election almost 50,000 electors throughout the Dominion cast their ballots for Labour candidates, so that hon. members can understand how few they are represented by, when there are only three Labour representatives in this house.
Since the opening of the session I have sat very patiently listening to speeches delivered by hon. members from all parts of the Dominion. I have listened to members from the maritimes outlining the conditions that exist in that part of the country. I have listened to their tales of. woe and of the bad conditions that prevail there. The mining industry is to-day in a very bad state in Nova Scotia and in other parts of eastern Canada. The men are living there by the grace of their friends and whatever they can get from other sources.. The mines are operating two or three days per month, and even at the present time a royal commission appointed by the Nova Scotia government is investigating two of the mines in order to find out why they are not operating on a better basis. That goes to show that the Duncan report of 1925 has not proved to be a solution of the mining problem in that province; conditions to-day being just about the same as they were prior to 1925.
I have listened this evening to the story of conditions in the fishing industry in Nova Scotia. I should like to have heard a little
more from the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) as to why the fishermen there receive approximately one cent per pound for their fish and by the time it comes to the consumer the latter has to pay anything from fifteen to thirty times as much for the same commodity.
I have also listened to members from Ontario telling us about the bad conditions that exist in that province, the large amount of unemployment in Toronto for instance, and the bad conditions among the farming community in the southern part of Ontario. I have listened to-day to the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) telling us about the bad conditions amongst the farmers in Manitoba. The provincial government of Manitoba have even asked the Dominion government to assist in giving relief to the unemployed in the urban centres of that province From Saskatchewan we have heard similar stories regarding the conditions of the farmers in that province.
When we come to Alberta we have heard similar stories from hon. members who represent that province in this house. We have been told about the bad conditions of the miners, about the unemployment in the cities, and the demand for a reduction in taxation on the necessaries of life. I listened the other day with a good deal of interest to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) who discussed the coal question and who demanded a national fuel policy. The same demand for a national fuel policy has been made by members in other parts of the house, but I have not yet heard it stated what they mean by a national fuel policy. Do they mean the nationalization of the mines in this Dominion, or do they mean something else?
I desire to make one or two remarks in connection with the Alberta coal situation, because one of the large consumers of Alberta coal is the province of Manitoba. Ten years ago Manitoba was using very little, if any, Alberta ooal. At the present time, as a result of the efforts of the Alberta government and efforts made in other directions, the domestic consumption of Alberta coal in Manitoba is approximately ninety per cent of the total. For that reason any action that is taken by the Alberta government or by this house in regard to the coal question, and particularly the Alberta coal question, is bound to be of interest to the people of Manitoba. The freight on coal is something which the people of Manitoba are interested in, and if the Dominion government or the railways are going to give a rate of $6.50 per ton on coal that is moved from Alberta right down, for
The Address-Mr. Heaps

instance, into the centre of Ontario, then the people of Manitoba will expect equal treatment to that given to the people of that province. If a ton of coal can be moved for 86.50 from Alberta to Ontario, there is no reason why it should cost $4.50 to move a ton of coal from Calgary to certain parts of Manitoba.
Alberta has thought fit at a recent session of the legislature to impose <a tax of five to nine cents per ton on all coal mined in that province. So far it has not been able to collect the tax because certain actions have been taken in the courts to test the legality of that legislation. As one representing the province of Manitoba I protest against legislation of that character. I cannot understand how a Farmer government, who have Farmer representatives in this house and who make speeches here objecting to taxing the necessities of life, can themselves tax a necessity of life for people in other parts of the Dominion of Canada. That tax of five to nine cents per ton which the Alberta government is endeavouring to impose upon coal mined in that province will add twenty-five cents per ton to every ton of coal sold, and will make it just so much more difficult for the mines of Alberta to compete with the mines of the United' States. On the other hand the Alberta government come to the Dominion authorities and ask them to reduce freight rates. Before they do that they should take every possible step to see that Alberta coal is mined in the most efficient way and given to the people at the lowest possible rates.
Another thing I should like to see the provincial government of Alberta do is this: For many yeaTS efforts have been made to find out the actual cost of mining a ton of coal in many of the Alberta mines, but so far those efforts have been unsuccessful. Apparently nobody can tell us exactly what it costs to mine a ton of coal in Alberta. It appears from the knowledge I have obtained that an obstacle has always been created when the question is one of getting this information from the proper authorities. I believe, however, the cost of coal at the mine mouth at Alberta is approximately $4.50 per ton, and I want to know why coal mined under similar circumstances in the United States, where wages are slightly higher than they are in Alberta, can be mined for one-half the cost in that province. The question arises in my mind whether they are using the most efficient methods for the production of coal in Alberta. I think when people in other parts of the Dominion are called to the
[Mr. Hpaps.l
assistance of Alberta, they ought to be given these facts, and it would not be amiss if the provincial government of Alberta attempted to furnish these facts to the people of the Dominion.
As I stated a few minutes ago, I have listened to speeches which various hon. members have delivered describing conditions existing in their respective provinces, and with the exception of a few speakers from the government side not a solitary member has spoken of the prosperity which, it is claimed in the speech from the throne, prevails at the present time in Canada. Each member has got up and told of the conditions that prevail in his own particular province, and it is very hard for me to reconcile the speeches made in this house, coming from the government side, from the opposition side and from the group in this corner, with the talk of prosperity in the speech from the throne. Ii there is prosperity, then I am sure that it is not reflected in the speeches that have come from every part of this chamber.
The speech from the throne deals very little with the future; it deals with the past. It is not a speech that looks forward; it is a speech that looks backward. I believe that statesmanship, as a rule does not take the backward view, but the forward view.
The things that are in the speech from-the throne I do not regard as of great and vital consequence. The important part of the speech refers to the appointment of ministers to France and Japan. I am sure that the unemployed of Winnipeg, the semiemployed miners of Nova Scotia, the fisherman who gets a cent a pound for his fish, and the unemployed in all parts of this Dominion, will feel that there is very little to rejoice over in the announcement that Canada is going to send ministers to France and Japan. That will neither fill their empty stomachs nor tell them where their next meal is to come from.
One^ omission from the speech from the throne, involving a matter which I think is of even greater consequence than the question of the appointment of two ministers abroad, is any reference to the reason why the Canadian government broke off friendly relations with soviet Russia. Both this session and last session we heard a great deal about the status of Canada. I am no great specialist on that question and do not understand it as deeply as some hon. members of this house do. But I am given to understand that one reason why the Dominion government broke off relations with Russia was because Great Britain had done

The Address-Mr. Heaps
so. The only excuse of this government, if I remember correctly, was that it had followed the example of Great Britain. During the last session of this house we were told that Canada had achieved a new status at the last Imperial conference, and yet almost immediately that new status had been achieved, at one of the very first opportunities the government had of showing that new status, it meekly followed the example of the British government. I want to congratulate, if I may, the_ new leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Bennett). I have been very much interested in the hon. member, interested long before I over dreamed that I would be a member of

I notice one other matter that is absent from the Conservative party platform, and that is the very good suggestion that the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) himself made in the house last year during the budget debate. On that occasion he suggested the conscription of money at four per cent; there is no such plank, however, in the Conservative party platform. If at any future time it is the fortune of the Conservative party to be the dominant party in this house, I trust that that particular suggestion of its leader will be put into effect.
There is one other statement- and I regret it exceedingly-that has been made by the hon. leader of the opposition in the course of the many speeches that he has made since he became the leader of his party. He has referred to the great asset that wealth is to a man in public life. I do not think wealth does give or ought to give priority to anyone who holds a responsible position in the public life of the Dominion of Canada. When the hon. leader of the opposition claims that the wealth he is fortunate enough to possess gives him a sort of prior claim to a position of responsibility, I think he is doing an injustice to a great many members of this house who are not so fortunate as to be possessed of any wealth at all. Wealth should give no prior rights to high office. In fact if we look at history we find that there have been very few really great men who have been wealthy and very few wealthy men who have been really great.

It has been admitted by the leader of the opposition that we are prosperous in this Dominion. I wonder who enjoys this prosperity. After we have listened to speeches by hon. gentlemen from all parts of the country no one will claim that the great masses of the people have benefited greatly by this so-called and one-sided prosperity. I believe the leader of the opposition is a director of one of the leading banks in this country, and a few weeks ago I read the annual report of this particular bank, covering a whole newspaper page, while at the same time, in the inside columns of the same eastern newspapers which carried this report, there appeared the story of an offence committed by an employee of this very bank. This particular employee, in his less thoughtful moments, had taken a few hundred dollars that belonged to the bank. He was a young man who had previously enjoyed an excellent reputation at the bank. Naturally he was arrested, and taken to court. He was about twenty years of age and it appeared m the course of the proceedings against him that prior to the Christmas festivities, while reflecting on the poverty in his own home, he was driven to desperation and took this money so that his own family might enjoy some of the good things which are customary at that time of the year. Then it came out that this young man, who occupied a fairly responsible position with the bank, was receiving $40 a month. Here we have in one column of a newspaper the report of the prosperity of this bank, while we find that, the employees who have helped to build up these huge surpluses are receiving such miserable salaries as $40 a month. Hank presidents will speak of prosperity, but this man who was receiving $40 a month must be typical of thousands of others in similar institutions who are living on a wage barely sufficient to keep body and soul together.

Four thousand dollars' worth of clear titled land in 1867 meant that a man must have a very considerable acreage before he could be' elevated to the other chamber in that period of Canada's history.
Canada at the present time is governed or partly governed by two houses. In one house we have a democratic body elected by the people of the Dominion, while on the other hand we have an autocratic assembly, an irresponsible body which can do as it pleases. It may veto legislation passed in this house just as often as it likes and yet we do not seem to be doing anything to ensure that the express wish of the people shall be carried into effect as the law of the land. I do not believe that in any country in which there is an elective system you will find a body appointed in the same way as our second chamber is in Canada; and sooner or later this other chamber of parliament will have to conform to the will of the people.
