The situation in the upper chamber to-day is such that it deserves some publicity. Thirty-two members of that honourable body are of the legal profession-thirty-two out of ninety-six. Twenty-five are directors of financial corporations; eighteen are merchants 56103-15
and manufacturers; six are medical men and eight are connected with the newspapers. The man who suggests that this body reflects the sentiments of this country is grossly mistaken and very far from the facts. Personally I am not in favour of a second chamber, but if there is to be one I think it should in some degree reflect the will of the people. It is all very well for hon. members to say that we must stand by the British North America Act. Let me say this in regard to that act: The British North America Act was made for the people of Canada and not the people of Canada for the British North America Act; and if the act does not conform to conditions as we find them in the country to-day, then we ought to amend it so as to bring it into conformity with existing conditions. Some of my hon. friends from the province of Quebec may be alarmed about any proposed amendments to the British North America Act. Let me assure them, as one member from the west, that there is no intention on the part of our western people to deprive the people of Quebec of any rights which may be guaranteed them under the act. Personally I should be entirely opposed to any attempt on the part of this house to infringe on any rights extended to the early settlers of this Dominion. At the same time, it would be unfair for any province, jealous as it may be of its own rights, to stand in the way of any attempt to amend the act to bring it more into conformity with modern conditions. There is nowhere in the world, so far as I am aware, a second chamber that has the powers which are enjoyed by the second chamber in Canada. It has been sometimes compared to the British House of Lords. But those who tell us that we should stand by the British North America Act overlook the fact that not more than seventeen years ago the British act governing the House of Lords was amended in respect of the relations between the two houses of parliament in Great Britain. In 1911 when the House of Lords attempted to veto certain legislation passed by the Commons, after they had rejected the budget, what happened? Immediately the Liberal Prime Minister of that day obtained from His Majesty a document empowering him to appoint to the House of Lords as many peers of the realm as might be necessary to over-ride the decision of that house, and that very threat to appoint several hundred gentlemen to the upper house disposed the lords to pass the measure which they had dared to reject. It took away their power of absolute veto. But we have no such right in Canada; we may pass legislation in this house a hundred times and have it re-

jected as often by the senate, if that body so wishes. Mr. LEO K. LAFLAMME (Montmagny) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of members, as it is my first attempt to address this house. As representative of the county of Montmagny, I wish to make a few remarks on the speech from the throne. I heartily associate myself with the members who have preceded me in this debate, to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both performed their task in a praiseworthy manner and the congratulations which were extended to them were well deserved.
First, the speech from the throne mentions the prosperous state of the country. By this it wishes to convey the idea of the general prosperity of our Canada. As stated by the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley), if prosperity is not everywhere felt, in each and every riding represented by the hon. members of this house, to the extent that we could say that conditions are very good and even of the very best, nevertheless we cannot deny that the country as a whole is certainly prosperous. If prosperity is not evident everywhere, if all and each of us can point out certain weaknesses in special cases, due to the fact that we meet in a house where every one comes from a different riding, and where also we must look after the general business of the country, we cannot however refrain from really agreeing upon that statement contained in the speech from the throne: that our country is prosperous and has been so during the last fiscal year of

1927. The statements contained in reports from bank presidents and various corporations, not only are optimistic but clearly testify that the country has enjoyed an unparalleled prosperity during this last year. I shall not further emphasize this point as the leader of the government has clearly exposed the situation, and has made us realize the optimism which every well thinking Canadian should feel when he considers the general conditions existing in our country.
Some have asserted that we had no reason to congratulate ourselves upon the year 1927 being the occasion of the celebration of the sixtieth anniversary of Canada's confederation. This event was an excellent opportunity for Canadians to look back somewhat on the past. In all parts of the country we celebrated this anniversary, because we felt the need of commemorating what our predecessors had done for our country. It was well to recall the work done by the advocates of British institutions, it was necessary to remind the present generation, the young people, those who will follow in our footsteps, of the work accomplished by our forefathers in the various spheres in which they were engaged; it was also right to recall the struggles that our forefathers had to undergo for the vindication of responsible government. Especially within these last years this topic has been discussed in various ways and form; it was therefore well to recall these heroic struggles for the conquest of responsible government in order to obtain in Canada the same rights as British subjects enjoy in England.
These celebrations were also an opportunity for many to recall that the pioneers of this country came from the province of Quebec. On that occasion of July 1st, 1927, the opportunity presented itself to point out that those who had laid the corner stone of the first edifice in a great number of Canadian cities, were French or descendants of Frenchmen. At a time when we were speaking of unity and ties which should exist between the various races, we from the province of Quebec could not wish for a better opportunity to recall that those who cleared the land, the pioneers of our country, were our ancestors, in order to impress upon those who to-day live with us in this vast Dominion, that when we display our true and sincere love for the Canadian soil, it is because we really feel at home and are conscious that we took root, here before any other.
A question of the utmost importance which should be borne in mind by Canadians, is that of immigration, as mentioned in the

speech from the throne. The hon. members who have preceded me in this debate, for the most part discussed it from their own viewpoint. This question of increasing our population raises a problem which interests every one of us. We should sincerely strive to build up our country, to increase its population so as to lessen the burdens which we are forced to carry, and we should also develop the natural resources of Canada. If we are to have an increase in population, we certainly should all have at heart that this increase reflects on the general welfare. If [DOT] we find it necessary to bring in immigrants from foreign countries, Europe, the British Isles and elsewhere, not only should we insist that they be physically fit and sound of mind, but we should also seek to induce people who can really become Canadian citizens and think like Canadians that are now living in this country, so that they may be assimilated and join us in the ascending march towards progress. The problem is indeed a very interesting one, and here the question arises whether we should not give preference to those who were born in our country, who are more likely to remain here and foster its development. We should endeavour to solve the problem by doing our best to keep at home those who are born here. This immigration problem is also linked with that of emigration. Canadian born citizens have a natural desire to remain here; they wish to develop and build up this country 'which is dear to them. We should therefore find the means to keep this desirable population here, at least all those among our people who wish to settle in this country so as to further its expansion. Individual wealth must certainly promote that end, in fact it does contribute to the general wealth of a country, if we have the right kind of people to develop our natural resources. The latter will be unlimited because people will interest themselves and they will thus help most effectively in the general development and increase of the wealth of our country.	[DOT]

The autonomy which they have acquired up to now, if it is not quite independence, has certainly created some embarrassment in the interpretation of international law. In certain spheres and in many aspects they are looked upon as sovereign states; as for instance, they can. negotiate their own treaties through a minister of their own, without the assistance of an English ambassador. One must bear in mind that always, in regard to international law, nations have proceeded byevolution and when a situation had materialized, the wording of the international law conformed itself afterwards with the existing situation.
